strengths: Significant computational acceleration: By evolving both the surrogate dynamics and the score-based filtering completely within a compact latent space (~10 dimensions), LD-EnSF avoids solving full high-dimensional PDEs during online filtering, achieving speedups of three to five orders of magnitude over full-space simulation.

Effective handling of extreme spatiotemporal sparsity: The integration of an LSTM encoder leveraging observation history resolves the ill-posedness and vanishing-score issues of standard EnSF when observations are extremely sparse (e.g., 0.44% spatial sensors) and noisy.

Joint state and parameter estimation: The formulation conveniently augments the latent space to jointly assimilate latent states and uncertain physical parameters (such as the Reynolds number or initial condition coordinates).
Clear writing and well-structured presentation, supported by comprehensive implementation and hyperparameter search details in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited comparative baselines: The empirical comparison is restricted to EnSF and Latent-EnSF. Given that latent-space data assimilation using EnKF and surrogate models is well established (e.g., Peyron et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2023), comparing against standard latent EnKF methods or other neural operator/surrogate DA pipelines would provide a more complete picture of the benefits of score filtering vs. ensemble Kalman filtering in latent space.

Limited parametric diversity and system complexity: The evaluation is conducted on relatively low-dimensional parameterizations (a 2D initial bump coordinate for shallow water equations and a scalar Reynolds number for Kolmogorov flow). It remains unclear whether the compact 9-10 dimensional LDNet latent representation scales effectively to broader parametric variability or chaotic systems with complex, distributed uncertainties.

Lack of targeted ablation studies: The paper attributes performance gains both to the LDNet formulation and to the temporal memory of the LSTM observation encoder. An explicit ablation comparing the LSTM encoder against a static frame-by-frame observation encoder (such as the VAE encoder used in Latent-EnSF) would help disentangle the individual benefits of each component.

Heuristic latent likelihood formulation: The observation update relies on treating the LSTM-mapped observation as an identity observation of the latent state with approximate additive noise. A deeper discussion on the theoretical consistency or calibration of the resulting latent posterior relative to the true physical Bayesian posterior would strengthen the foundational methodology.

strengths: Clear motivation and pipeline: By performing both dynamic propagation and observation assimilation entirely in a low-dimensional latent space, the proposed LD-EnSF overcomes the primary computational bottleneck of Latent-EnSF (which required running the full PDE numerical solver at each assimilation step).

Substantial computational acceleration: Demonstrates several orders of magnitude speedup in forward dynamics simulation (up to ~10^5-fold for Kolmogorov flow) and lower filtering time due to operating in a ~10-dimensional latent space.
Effective temporal encoding: Using an LSTM to encode the history of sparse observations improves robustness against observation noise and spatial sparsity compared to single-frame VAE encoders.
Joint state and parameter estimation: The framework naturally estimates uncertain physical parameters (e.g., initial bump location, Reynolds number) concurrently with latent states.

Thorough empirical evaluation: Validated on two standard fluid dynamical benchmarks (shallow water equations and Kolmogorov flow) under severe observation sparsity (0.44% spatial coverage) and significant noise levels (up to 20%).
weaknesses: Incremental architectural novelty: The core contribution is largely an effective synthesis of existing components (LDNets, EnSF, and LSTMs) with modest adjustments, such as the two-stage LDNet training and shifted initial latent indexing.

Missing traditional and modern latent DA baselines: The comparison is restricted to standard EnSF and Latent-EnSF. It lacks comparison against established latent assimilation methods (e.g., Latent Ensemble Kalman Filters / Reduced-Order EnKF or score-based sequential Langevin filters cited in the literature review).

Heuristic latent noise treatment: In Eq. (18), the observation model is assumed to have additive latent noise obtained by mapping observation noise through the LSTM. A more rigorous mathematical justification or characterization of the resulting latent likelihood and its covariance structure would strengthen the methodological foundation.

Relatively low parameter complexity: The parametric uncertainty considered is low-dimensional (2D initial condition center for shallow water, 1D Reynolds number for Kolmogorov flow). It remains unclear how well the approach scales to high-dimensional parameter spaces or distributed spatial parameter fields.

strengths: Addresses a significant computational bottleneck in ensemble-based data assimilation (DA) by replacing expensive full-order numerical PDE solvers with a fast, low-dimensional latent dynamical surrogate (LDNet).
Integrating an LSTM encoder to condition latent states on multi-step observation history is a well-motivated strategy to handle both high spatial and temporal observation sparsity.

Demonstrates substantial online runtime speedups (orders of magnitude faster than full-space simulation and Latent-EnSF) while achieving lower reconstruction RMSE on two standard benchmark physical systems (shallow water equations and Kolmogorov flow).
Successfully extends the assimilation framework to perform joint state and parameter estimation within the low-dimensional latent space.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: The core contribution primarily combines existing building blocks—LDNets (Regazzoni et al., 2024), EnSF (Bao et al., 2024), and standard LSTM sequence encoders—with relatively minor modifications such as shifted initial conditions and a two-stage retraining schedule.

Restrictive experimental setup relying on low-dimensional parameterizations: In the shallow water setup, variability is governed merely by the 2D coordinates of an initial Gaussian bump; in Kolmogorov flow, only the scalar Reynolds number is varied while the initial state is fixed. This significantly simplifies the dynamics onto an unnaturally low-dimensional manifold, leaving open whether the approach scales to arbitrary, high-dimensional uncertain initial conditions encountered in realistic DA scenarios.

Missing standard and competitive data assimilation baselines: The comparison is restricted to vanilla EnSF and Latent-EnSF. Classical and widely adopted DA methods (e.g., Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF/LETKF) with covariance localization/inflation, or 4D-Var) as well as other latent-space DA surrogates (e.g., Peyron et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024) are omitted.

Unclear formulation and characterization of the latent observation likelihood: In Section 3.3, the observation model assumes an identity mapping in latent space with noise estimated by the LSTM encoding. The paper lacks a rigorous mathematical justification and empirical analysis of how the resulting non-trivial distribution of latent noise affects the score function computation and posterior sampling accuracy.

Evaluation protocol questions regarding observation noise: The LSTM encoder is trained exclusively on noiseless observations (Section 4.3), yet evaluated on observations with up to 20% noise. The rationale behind omitting noise during training is insufficiently justified, and ablations regarding training with noisy data are missing.

strengths: Clear motivation and pipeline: Conducting the entire data assimilation cycle—both filtering and forward dynamic propagation—within a compact latent space effectively resolves the major computational bottleneck of existing score-based DA methods like Latent-EnSF.

Methodological improvements: The paper makes sensible enhancements to LDNets (shifting initial latent states, two-stage fine-tuning, Fourier embeddings, and ResNet architectures) and integrates an LSTM encoder to process historical sparse observations and jointly estimate uncertain system parameters.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Experiments across three complex dynamical benchmarks (Kolmogorov flow, shallow water tsunami equations, and atmospheric PlanetSWE) show orders-of-magnitude computational speedups while achieving superior or comparable accuracy against strong baselines including LETKF, vanilla EnSF, and Latent-EnSF.

Thorough sensitivity and ablation analysis: The appendices provide detailed explorations of latent dimensionality, ensemble sizes, observation density, noise misspecification (including non-Gaussian and heteroskedastic noise), and out-of-distribution shifts.
weaknesses: Observation operator inflexibility: As acknowledged in Appendix E.4, the LSTM observation encoder is fixed to a predetermined set of sensor locations, requiring retraining if sensor locations change or if observations are irregularly missing across time cycles. This limits practical applicability in operational settings with dynamic sensor networks.

Justification of EnSF in the latent space: Since the latent observation operator is modeled as the identity map ($H_{\text{latent}}(\kappa_t) = \kappa_t$) with an additive estimated Gaussian noise $\hat{\gamma}_t$, the update step is essentially linear in the latent space. The paper does not thoroughly compare or ablate EnSF against simpler latent filtering techniques (such as an ensemble Kalman filter in the compact latent space) to demonstrate whether the reverse-time SDE diffusion update remains necessary once inside a well-behaved latent space.

Parametric scope: The framework focuses predominantly on static or slowly-varying system parameters $u$, which restricts the problem formulation to systems where uncertainties can be parameterized compactly (e.g., scalar Reynolds number or static initial condition center).

strengths: Compelling and principled motivation: The paper tackles a critical computational bottleneck in modern data assimilation—the requirement of expensive forward numerical solvers within the ensemble filtering loop—by carrying out both the dynamics propagation and the score-based filtering entirely within a compact latent space.

Well-designed technical approach: The proposed extensions to Latent Dynamics Networks (LDNets)—such as shifted initial latent states, two-stage fine-tuning, and Fourier/ResNet spatial decoders—produce smooth, low-dimensional latent trajectories that overcome the oscillatory dynamics typical of standard autoencoders. Pairing this with a history-aware LSTM encoder allows effective joint estimation of latent states and uncertain physical parameters from sparse, irregular observations.

Dramatic computational gains: Eliminating full-state numerical solves during the online filtering loop yields speedups of 3 to 5 orders of magnitude in forward propagation time ($T_d$) across three diverse benchmark problems, making real-time ensemble filtering practically viable.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: The method is validated on three challenging dynamical systems (Kolmogorov flow, shallow water tsunami equations, and spherical atmospheric modeling PlanetSWE) under extreme spatial (~0.1%) and temporal (~0.2%) observation sparsity, consistently outperforming EnSF, Latent-EnSF, and LETKF.

Extensive ablation and robustness analysis: The appendices provide deep insights, exploring non-Gaussian/heteroskedastic noise, out-of-distribution initializations, surrogate training strategies, observation encoder architectures (LSTM vs. CNN), and sensitivity to latent dimension and ensemble size.
weaknesses: Surrogate distribution and domain shift limitations: As demonstrated in Appendix E.3, the accuracy of LDNet and the resulting assimilation degrades when the true state wanders outside the support of the offline training data. In highly chaotic systems or open-ended geophysical regimes, surrogate generalization remains a fundamental constraint.

Sensor layout dependency: While the LSTM encoder supports unstructured/irregular observation networks, the model must be retrained whenever the physical sensor configuration changes significantly, as noted in Appendix E.4. Developing a sensor-agnostic or set-based observation encoder (e.g., using cross-attention or Graph Neural Networks) would enhance flexibility.

Parameter dynamics scope: The parameter assimilation experiments primarily focus on static or slowly varying scalar/vector parameters (Reynolds number, tsunami bump coordinates, forcing parameters). Extending the framework to high-dimensional or rapidly evolving distributed parameter fields is discussed but not yet demonstrated.

Uncertainty quantification calibration: Although RMSE and CRPS are reported across varying ensemble sizes, more thorough validation of posterior ensemble calibration (such as rank histograms or spread-error consistency over long assimilation windows) would strengthen the probabilistic claims.

strengths: Compelling computational speedup: By performing both state propagation and filtering entirely in a compact latent space via learned Latent Dynamics Networks (LDNets), the method eliminates the requirement of running expensive numerical PDE solvers online, achieving speedups of several orders of magnitude over standard full-space EnSF, Latent-EnSF, and LETKF.

Well-motivated architectural extensions: Enhancements to the base LDNet architecture—including shifting the initial latent state to accommodate varying initial conditions, two-stage fine-tuning of the decoder, and integrating Fourier positional encodings with ResNet blocks—provide clear and measurable gains in surrogate modeling fidelity.

Effective observation handling via temporal encoding: Replacing the static VAE observation encoder with an LSTM-based sequential encoder allows the model to leverage temporal correlations (time-delay embeddings) and perform joint state-parameter estimation under severe spatial and temporal observation sparsity.

Thorough experimental validation and ablations: The evaluation spans three diverse and challenging dynamical systems (Kolmogorov turbulent flow, shallow-water tsunami wave propagation, and spherical PlanetSWE atmospheric dynamics). The appendix includes extensive analyses covering observation density, ensemble size sensitivity, surrogate fidelity, non-Gaussian/heteroskedastic noise, out-of-distribution shifts, and module-level ablations.
weaknesses: Rigidity of the observation encoder to sensor geometry: The LSTM observation encoder takes a fixed-dimension flattened observation vector as input. Consequently, any alteration in sensor placement, missing observations, or variable sensor counts requires retraining the encoder from scratch, limiting practical flexibility compared to coordinate-based or graph-based encoders.

Heuristic latent noise formulation: The observation equation in the latent space (Eq. 8) assumes an identity observation operator with additive latent noise estimated via empirical sample variance on validation data. While empirically effective, this is a heuristic surrogate likelihood that decouples the filtering step from the rigorous physical observation likelihood.

Restriction to static or low-dimensional parametric uncertainty: The parameter estimation capability is primarily demonstrated on low-dimensional constant parameters (e.g., Reynolds number, initial bump center, forcing amplitude). In practical operational data assimilation, model errors are spatially distributed, dynamic, and stochastic, which poses substantial challenges for compact latent dynamics representations.

Incremental combination of existing components: Conceptually, the work is an integration of LDNets (Regazzoni et al., 2024) and Ensemble Score Filters (Bao et al., 2024b; Si & Chen, 2025) linked via an LSTM encoder. While the empirical execution is strong, the algorithmic novelty in the score-based filtering formulation itself is relatively modest.
